name: Zane Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing computer science in Manchester and I live in a flat in Fallowfield with three others. A normal week is lectures on algorithms and databases, then most evenings I'm building a side project, a little app that helps students spot dodgy landlord clauses in tenancy agreements. I use AI tools all day, for explaining concepts, for debugging, for drafting the app's text. Mum's a GP and Dad's a dentist, so they pay for everything, and I'm trying not to waste that. I also run a small coding club for first-years on Wednesdays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with five pictures of the next few years. This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, it's a useful tool and not a god. I'd tell the coding club to keep learning fundamentals because tools come and go. Online I'd post something like 'ok so that was a lot of noise for a good autocomplete'.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be a bit disappointed, which is weird. I find the big changes exciting, and a plateau means my generation doesn't get to build the new world. But my first job is safer, and that matters when Mum asks about my plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep building the tenancy app and try to get twenty students using it before Christmas. I'd apply for a summer internship at a startup in the Northern Quarter. And I'd keep using the tools, because they're still useful even if they're not magic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit restless. Nothing's under threat, but I'd miss the sense of something big happening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be disappointed. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You said you'd be disappointed. Why? Because I picked computing partly to be around something huge. A normal market means a normal grad job, and I could do that by being average.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do to avoid being average?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you do to avoid being average? Ship things. A working app with real users beats a good grade, and that's true with or without AI.

say: I'd say it's a **useful tool**, not a god.
I'd tell the coding club to learn **fundamentals**, because tools come and go.
think: A plateau means my **first job** is safer, which matters when Mum asks my plan.
I'd be a bit **disappointed**, since I like big changes.
do: Keep building the **tenancy app** and aim for twenty student users by Christmas.
Apply for a summer **internship** at a startup in the Northern Quarter.
S0.quote: A working app with real users beats a good grade, and that's true with or without AI.
fieldNote: Zane is a builder first; a **calm world** feels slightly dull to him.
His safety net is his parents' income, which keeps his mood calm.
He measures himself by shipped projects, not marks.

steps.text: Get twenty students using the tenancy app before Christmas
Apply for a summer internship at a Northern Quarter startup
Keep using AI tools daily for debugging and drafting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, finally, and we should be ready for the messy part. At the coding club I'd show people how to use the tools well, and online I'd argue that jobs will change, not vanish. I'd also say the gains should be shared, because a progressive view isn't just a label for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think my junior tasks, the small features and tests, get done by machines first. But I already use these tools every day, so I'd rather be the person who directs the tools than the person who competes with them. Still, there'd be fewer places for people who can't or won't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd turn the tenancy app into something that earns, maybe a small fee from letting agents. I'd learn to build with AI agents, not just chat with them, and read the papers behind them. I'd also pitch a talk at the university's careers week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, with a small knot in my stomach. I feel ahead of most people, which is a good feeling, but I can see friends on other courses who aren't, and that bothers me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which friends worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Which friends worry you? My flatmate Priya does marketing and her course is mostly writing. She says the first-year essays can be done in a minute by machine and she wonders what her degree is for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Priya?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you tell Priya? To learn the tools the way I did, by making something useful. But I'd also tell her it's not her fault if firms stop hiring juniors.

say: I'd say **good, finally**, and we should be ready for the messy part.
I'd argue jobs will **change**, not vanish, and gains should be shared.
think: My **junior tasks**, small features and tests, go to machines first.
I'd rather be the person who **directs** the tools.
do: Turn the tenancy app into a **small earner** with a fee for letting agents.
Learn to build with **AI agents**, not just chat with them.
Pitch a talk for the university's **careers week**.
feel: **Excited** with a small knot in my stomach for friends who aren't ready.
S1.quote: I'd rather be the person who directs the tools than the person who competes with them.
fieldNote: Zane feels **ahead** of peers, and it comes with guilt towards friends on other courses.
He ties his progressive politics to sharing gains.
His side project turns into a possible income.

steps.text: Add a small fee for letting agents to the tenancy app
Build a simple AI agent that reads tenancy contracts
Pitch a careers week talk on using AI tools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a public plan right now: income support, a seat at the table for workers, and rules on the biggest companies. And I'd say it with a real petition. Being excited and being scared aren't opposites, and I'd say that out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be rattled. Entry-level jobs would go first and I'd graduate into almost none. I'm comfortable with tools, so I'd manage better than most, but 'better than most' isn't a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go all in on the app, because building something of my own is the one route that doesn't depend on a hiring manager. I'd ask my parents to let me keep the fees as a safety net rather than switch. I'd also start a small campaign for a student basic income with Priya and the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, not frozen. I'd be wired and awake, like before a big launch, with a sour taste at the back of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the app doesn't work out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What happens if the app doesn't work out? Then I'd lean on my parents for a year and apply for anything hands-on, like robotics firms, since robots arrive three years later. I wouldn't be proud of it, but I'd do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your mum, the GP?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you say to your mum, the GP? I'd ask what her colleagues think, because medicine is partly thinking work too. She'd say patients still want a person in the room, and I'd love to believe her.

say: I'd say we need a **public plan** now: income support, worker seats, rules for big firms.
I'd say being excited and being scared **aren't opposites**.
think: Entry-level jobs would go first and I'd graduate into almost **none**.
Being **better than most** isn't a job.
do: Go **all in** on the tenancy app as my own route.
Start a **student basic income** campaign with Priya and the union.
Lean on my parents for a year if the app **fails**.
feel: **Anxious**, not frozen, wired like before a big launch.
S2.quote: Being excited and being scared aren't opposites, and I'd say that out loud.
fieldNote: He turns anxious but **acts quickly**, putting weight on the app and on politics.
He admits that being skilled doesn't guarantee a job.
Family cushion is his fallback, which he accepts with some shame.

steps.text: Spend evenings shipping the tenancy app to more cities
Start a student basic income petition with Priya
Apply for robotics firms if the app fails
Ask my parents to keep fees funded as a fallback

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to build things and to argue for rules, so we should do both. I'd tell the coding club that by 2031 the people who can direct these systems will matter most. And I'd say it publicly so people can argue back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel it's a race I can win partly. I'd graduate in 2029 or 2030, right before the date, and I'd have the app and a couple of internships behind me. That's not safety, but it's better than a blank page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and do two internships, ideally one at an AI lab and one at a hardware company. I'd keep growing the app and try to turn it into a small company before graduation. And I'd put aside part of whatever it earns, in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy and a bit buzzing. It's a big thing coming with a date on it, and I like having a date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would 'in case' look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would 'in case' look like? A year of rent, no more. I'd rather have the freedom to take a risk than a mountain of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about the most by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Who would you worry about the most by then? Probably people who didn't see it coming, like my cousins who work in call centres. I'd want to help them learn, but I'm not sure who'd listen to me.

say: I'd say five years is time to **build things** and argue for rules.
I'd say people who can **direct** these systems will matter most.
think: It's a **race** I can partly win.
I'd arrive at the date with an **app** and two internships behind me.
do: Finish the degree with **two internships**, one at an AI lab.
Grow the app into a **small company** before graduation.
Set aside a **year of rent** from what it earns.
feel: **Uneasy** and buzzing, because the date gives me something to aim at.
S3.quote: I'd rather have the freedom to take a risk than a mountain of savings.
fieldNote: Zane likes the **date**: a deadline gives him something to build against.
He thinks about his cousins in call centres, who are most exposed.
His savings plan is deliberately small to protect risk-taking.

steps.text: Do an internship at an AI lab in the summer
Turn the tenancy app into a registered small company
Save one year of rent from the app's earnings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long runway, and the question is who gets to use it. I'd say we should be building retraining and fair pay now. And I'd say it with a joke, so people actually listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel almost relaxed. I'd be 28 by 2036, with years of experience, maybe a company. The thing is, I'd also see how easy it is for people my age to drift for ten years and wake up unprepared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and work at a startup for two or three years. I'd keep building small products and probably start a company with friends around 25. I'd keep learning every new tool the day it comes out, because that's just how I'm built.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and curious. Ten years feels like a chapter, not a cliff, and I'm good with chapters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you less relaxed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would make you less relaxed? If governments did nothing and a few firms owned everything. Then I'd be okay, but my friends wouldn't. Being okay while my friends are not okay is hard to enjoy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What advice would you give to a first-year then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What advice would you give to a first-year then? Make things, not just notes. And find three people who disagree with you and keep them close.

say: I'd say ten years is a **long runway**; the question is who gets to use it.
I'd push for **retraining** and fair pay now.
think: I'd feel almost **relaxed**, with years of experience by 28.
The risk is people who **drift** for ten years and wake up unprepared.
do: Finish the degree and work at a **startup** for two or three years.
Start a **company** with friends around age 25.
Try every new **tool** the day it comes out.
feel: **Calm** and curious; ten years feels like a chapter, not a cliff.
S4.quote: Being okay while my friends are not okay is hard to enjoy.
fieldNote: More time gives Zane **calm** and room for risk.
His guilt about friends who are less ready shapes his politics.
He sees early tool adoption as a core part of his identity.

steps.text: Join a startup after graduating and stay two years
Start a company with friends around age 25
Test every new AI tool in my side projects

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, no question. I'd be fine compared to most, but I'd see friends like Priya graduating into nothing, and I'd hate how fast it came. What would help is income support, rules on the big firms and universities that teach how to use the tools instead of banning them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe: you asked what I'd do, but not who I'd do it with. I think the people who come through well are the ones with friends who share what they learn.

headlineQuote: The people who come through well are the ones with friends who share what they learn.
portrait: Zane is an 18-year-old **computer science** student in Manchester who uses AI tools all day and builds a tenancy-checking app.
Both parents are doctors who pay for everything, so his **cushion is strong** and he can take risks.
He is progressive and **adaptive**: he moves first, and worries about friends who can't.
His mood stays calm until the 2028 date, where he turns **anxious** and starts campaigning.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most, because friends like Priya would graduate into nothing.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **income support**, rules on big firms and universities that teach the tools.
